quick_answer: The Rhumb Line Bearing Calculator computes the constant compass bearing of a rhumb-line (loxodrome) course between two coordinates — the single heading a vessel or aircraft can steer without adjustment. Enter the start and end points and read the unchanging bearing, the course traditional navigation is built on.

On legs of a few hundred miles the two courses nearly coincide, and the constant heading wins on simplicity — fishing, coastal sailing and local flying live here.
Software that draws 'straight' lines on Mercator maps draws rhumbs. Knowing the bearing explains why the line between two cities bows the way it does.

The rhumb bearing from Heathrow's area to New York is about 257.9° held constant, versus a great-circle initial bearing near 287.9° that swings through the flight. One number you can steer; one shortest path you must keep correcting toward.

Extend any rhumb line far enough and it spirals into the pole — a loxodrome with a non-cardinal bearing never stops circling. Bearings due north, south, east or west are the exceptions that run straight.

faq: What is a rhumb line in plain terms?
A path that crosses every meridian at the same angle — a constant compass course. On Mercator charts it draws as a straight line, which is why navigators loved it for four centuries.
Is the rhumb bearing the shortest course?
No — the great circle is shortest. The rhumb trades a little distance (about 1% New York–Los Angeles, about 4% across the Atlantic) for a heading that never needs adjusting.
When are the two bearings equal?
Along a meridian (due north/south) and along the equator (due east/west) the rhumb and great circle coincide. Everywhere else they part, politely at first.
Does the bearing use true or magnetic north?
True north, like all bearings on this site. Apply local magnetic declination before steering by a physical compass.
Rhumb lines spiral toward the pole without reaching it (except due-north courses). Polar navigation uses grid navigation instead — a different instrument for a different ocean of ice.
Can a rhumb line cross the date line?
Yes — the calculator takes the longitude difference the short way, so Pacific crossings produce sensible constant bearings.
